### feat: a cycle's state is recorded, and every end is durable

(wink + agent, 2026-11-15 and 16, from the dead-end **fix: a cycle commit marks no rung current**,
io-uring-x1's `m-13`, and zc-ring-x1's `m-14`) The cycle protocol's next form, folding the three
entries the dead-end filed, **feat: a rung's state is recorded in TODO.md**, **feat: a closing names
its shape, and its target once**, and **feat: a dead-end lands on a target or a tag**. vc-x1 infers
a cycle's commits from bookmark reachability, so a set-aside bookmark corrupted the ladder and the
commit count twice. `cycle --commit` writes the next rung `(current)`, a prediction. And a cycle
stopped early has no durable end, its agent commits' `ochid:` trailers left naming work commits no
pushed ref keeps. One cycle, its rungs below, wink's "we'll see how it goes".

- **The principle.** The repo holds what happened, and `TODO.md` holds where the cycle is going and
  which commit each finished rung is. Every stage checks that the two agree, and a disagreement
  stops it, neither side assumed right.
  - The one inference that goes is the branch revset: the cycle's commits are the change ids its
    record holds, each confirmed by the repo.
  - `zTOC.md`'s ladder is generated from the record by every cycle command, never edited by hand.
- **The record.** A fenced `toml` block follows the `###` cycle heading, and one follows each
  `#####` rung heading once the rung has started.
  - The cycle block: `bookmark`, the cycle's one bookmark, `provisional = true` while that name is
    vc-x1's placeholder, and `state`, `done` or `dead-end`, added by the closing.
  - The rung block: `state`, one of `current`, `done`, or `dead-end`, `change`, the work commit's
    full change id for `done` and `dead-end`, and `agent-at`, the agent `@`'s commit id when the
    rung started, a commit id since it changes with every snapshot.
  - `current` and `agent-at` live in the working copy alone, `--commit` replacing them, so a commit
    holds `state` and `change` only.
  - No number is stored, the ladder numbering by position.
- **The invariants**, checked by every stage before it writes:
  - Order: the opening, the `done` and `dead-end` rungs in commit order, at most one `current`, the
    rungs not started, and the closing. No rung is inserted above a done one.
  - Resolves: each `change` is one visible commit, not divergent, titled as its heading.
  - Chain: each rung's commit is the next one's parent, the last being `@-`, the tip.
  - Nothing unrecorded: `opening::@- ~ <recorded>` is empty. A hand `jj commit` in the chain is
    refused, naming the fix, and local-ladder intermediates are reported as not yet collapsed,
    `--commit` waiting for them.
  - Done is frozen (wink): a `done` or `dead-end` rung's heading and block match its own commit's,
    never deleted or changed, the prose under them editable, and vc-x1 refuses to continue until
    one changed is restored. Done rungs are not renamed, unpublished ones included.
  - Generated: `zTOC.md`'s ladder is the one the committed record or the working copy's makes, any
    other a hand edit, refused, the fix being an edit of `TODO.md`.
  - Bookmark: the cycle's bookmark is on the tip, and a move is reported.
  - Heads: vc-x1 commits on the cycle's chain alone, and `--status` reports a head forking off it.
    `--close` refuses while a work commit an agent commit names is reachable from neither the
    closing nor a pushed ref, joining it by `--close <REV,...>` or tagging it clearing that.
- **Starting a cycle.** `--open` needs nothing, and over a cycle in progress it makes nothing and
  prints the ways to end it.
  - Without `--title` the heading is the placeholder `### (untitled)`, editable until the opening
    commits, whose `--commit` refuses the placeholder. The opening's heading is then frozen and the
    closing pairs with it, the `###` heading still free to drift.
  - Without `--bookmark` the bookmark is provisional, `cycle-<ts>`, `<ts>` UTC to the second in ISO
    8601's basic form, and renamed to the title's slug when the opening commits. A name the user
    gave is never renamed.
  - `--bookmark-rename <new>` renames the cycle's bookmark on any stage, the record with it, free
    before a draft push and a push after one, its approval asked.
  - `--bookmark` on the later stages, which today names the cycle, goes, the record holding it.
- **The rung lifecycle.** A rung is any work or experiment, with the agent's help or without.
  `--rung-start` and `--rung-stop` edit `TODO.md` and `zTOC.md` in the work `@` and make no commit,
  so a rung in flight shows in the ladder.
  - `--rung-start` marks a rung `current` and records `agent-at`: the first rung not started, or
    `--title`'s, moved up to be next with its subsection. `--title X --insert` adds a heading as the
    next rung, so a ladder is built as it goes. Refused while a rung is current.
  - `--rung-stop` returns the current rung to not started, its edits left alone.
  - `--commit` commits the current rung or `--title`'s, writing `done` and `@`'s change id, and is
    refused with no rung in flight and no `--title`.
  - `--commit --dead-end` commits a rung given up, its attempt kept in history, then inserts and
    starts `revert: <rung title>`, `@` restored to the parent's tree but for the record and the
    version file, so the revert is its own reviewed commit.
  - The quick path: `--open`, `--commit --title "..."` for the opening, then for each rung
    `--rung-start --insert --title "..."`, the work, and `--commit`.
- **Scopes and pairing.** `-s u`, unpaired, joins `b`, `w`, `a`, and `p`, taken by `commit`,
  `squash`, `cycle --commit`, and `cycle --close`.
  - `u` is the work-repo of a dual workspace committed with no trailer and never covered. `p` is a
    plain repo, with no agent-repo, and stays refused on a dual workspace's sides. In a line: `p`
    says there is no agent-repo here, `u` that there is one and this commit does not involve it.
  - The scope is chosen at the commit, by what happened: `-s b` when the agent helped, `-s u` when
    it did not, and `-s w` for the N:1 case. `-s u` warns when the agent `@` differs from the
    rung's `agent-at`, a session having written during the rung.
  - The Land commits the agent `@` for the work commits with a forward `ochid:` alone, so a cycle of
    unpaired commits makes no agent commit.
  - The durability obligation starts at a paired commit: a work commit an agent commit names stays
    reachable from a pushed ref, landed, kept as a `dead-end` rung of a landed or tagged cycle, or
    tagged. An unpaired commit, or an experiment never committed, is kept or dropped freely.
- **The closing.** The shape is declared at the closing.
  - `--close --multi-step` takes `--trapezoid [<target>]` or `--linear`, and a bare one is refused.
    `--trapezoid` takes its target from `--land <target>` when it has none, `--trapezoid A --land B`
    is refused, and `--linear` takes none. The conflicting flags are refused as they are parsed.
  - The shape is checked against the count of the recorded commits.
  - A done closing is refused while a work rung is current or not started: commit it, dead-end it,
    or delete it, a rung not started always deletable.
  - A dead-end closing, `--close --multi-step --dead-end [--revert]`, leaves the rungs not started
    in the record unmarked, refuses a current one, and renames the closing heading `<cycle title>
    dead-end closing` before its commit, so the ladder names the commit's title. `--revert`
    restores the opening's parent tree but for the record and the version file, which still moves
    forward.
- **How a cycle ends.** Durable is reachable from a pushed ref, a remote keeping no commit without
  one, and a tag is the ref for a dead-end not landed.

| # | How the cycle ends | Durable by | The next cycle begins | `--yes` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `--close --multi-step [--dead-end] --trapezoid\|--linear --land <target> [--push]` | the target, and its version tag | `--open` | no |
| 2 | `--close --multi-step --dead-end --tag [<name>] [--push]` | the dead-end tag | `--open --from <target>` | no |
| 3 | `--close --multi-step --dead-end --no-tag` | nothing, until a tag is pushed | `--open --from <target>` | yes |
| 4 | nothing committed | nothing needed | `--open` | no |
| 5 | outside the tool: `jj abandon`, a bookmark deleted | none | anything | cannot ask |

- **The tags.**
  - The version tag, `m-14`'s ask: `--land <target>` tags the commit the target moves to
    `v<version>`, read by `[version]`'s `file` and `pattern`, `[land] tag = "v{version}"` setting
    the form. `--no-tag` skips it, a tag at the same commit is a no-op, one at another commit is
    refused naming both, and a workspace with no `[version]` gets none, said. A landed dead-end is
    tagged too, its version having moved forward.
  - Tags are lightweight, made by jj-lib with no git spawn, the tagged commit's title saying what it
    is.
  - The dead-end tag is named `dead-end-<ts>`, `<name>`, or `<name>-<ts>`, `<ts>` UTC to the
    millisecond in ISO 8601's basic form, `20261116T215837.123Z`, since a ref holds no `:`. A name
    taken, locally or on the remote, is refused. `--tag-dead-end <rev> [<name>]` tags a closed
    dead-end after the fact, row 3 becoming row 2.
  - A work-repo push carries the local tags `origin` lacks, listed in its plan and `--dry-run`, tags
    first, a clash stopping it. The work-repo alone is tagged, agent commits being on the agent
    `main`.
- **After a dead-end.**
  - `--push` is the publish, as on every stage, so a dead-end is reviewed locally first.
  - `--open --from <target>` follows an unlanded dead-end. It prints the dead-end's version and
    refuses an opening whose version is not above it, so no `X.Y.Z-N` is built twice. It brings
    forward the dead-end closing's `## Continuation notes`, `## Todo`, and `## Waiting` when the
    target is where the dead-end opened, and is refused otherwise, those carried by hand.
  - An agent push names the agent commits whose `ochid:` resolves to nothing on the remote, from row
    3 or 5, and pushes anyway: the agent-repo stays whole, and the session is found from the
    work-repo by time.
- **Reports.** `--status` reads the record: the ladder, the rung in flight, the commits not pushed,
  each failing invariant with its fix, the forked heads, and a dead-end not durable, the last two
  also reported by the acquaint repo check and `--open`. Every new flag completes its values by
  `clap_complete`'s dynamic completers: the targets, the rungs not started, the default tag name,
  and the dead-ends not tagged.
- **Migration.** A cycle in progress whose record has no blocks is migrated once, by the first stage
  that runs, its done rungs' blocks taken from the old branch revset, the inference's last use, and
  an ambiguous one refused. This cycle migrates itself once the recorded-state rung's dev build
  takes over.
- **The agent-files**, to `v0.3.1-15`: `AGENTS.md`'s Cycle-record, Cycle shape, Unplanned work, the
  per-rung flow, Committing vs pushing, Close-out, and the rules index, `jj.md`'s Land and push,
  `notes.md`'s In Progress block and zTOC format, and `cycle-model.md`'s specimens, a dead-end rung,
  an unpaired rung, and an unlanded dead-end among them.
- **The rungs**, provisional, between the opening and the closing:
  - `feat: a rung's state is recorded in TODO.md`
  - `feat: cycle --rung-start, --rung-stop, and --commit by the rung in flight`
  - `feat: -s u commits the work-repo unpaired`
  - `feat: the cycle's bookmark is provisional, renamed by --bookmark-rename`
  - `feat: a closing names its shape, and its target once`
  - `feat: a dead-end rung and a dead-end cycle revert`
  - `feat: land tags the version, and a dead-end lands on a target or a tag`
  - `feat: open over a cycle in progress, and open --from`
  - `feat: reports name forked heads and dead-ends not durable`
  - `docs: the agent-files record a cycle's state`
- **Considered and not taken:**
  - `zTOC.toml` or `zTOC.json` as the record, wink's first thought, a second source beside
    `TODO.md`.
  - Cutting the branch only at bookmarks not descending from the opening, still an inference.
  - Storing rung numbers, which shift on every insert.
  - `cycle --start`, reading too like `--open`, and `rung start`, a positional verb.
  - `--commit` taking the first rung not started, a guessed rung being the bug this removes.
  - Always a trapezoid, each rung's commit the merge (wink's thought): it rewrites the previous
    rung at every commit, and a closing with `--land` lands at any rung without that.
  - `-s p` meaning unpaired in a dual workspace, which loses the refusal that catches `p` in the
    wrong place, and the scope defaulted from `CLAUDECODE`, which says who typed the command, not
    whether the agent helped.
  - `--open` closing a cycle in progress as a dead-end, too easy, wink's, and the next cycle stacked
    on the dead-end, which lands it unasked.
  - `--push-dead-end`, wink's lean, `--push` kept so a dead-end is reviewed before it is published.
  - Annotated tags, which jj-lib does not make, so a git spawn against `clippy.toml`'s register.
- **Carried and left out.**
  - A block per rung is a trial, wink's "see how the noise feels".
  - The dead-end's rungs 1 and 2 hold the `(done)`-only ladder and its tests to take back, and its
    closing rung says what today's dead-end path taught. `m-13` and `m-14` are told when it lands.
  - Out of it, each its own entry: **feat: a short form for ending a cycle**, **feat: a cycle takes
    an added bookmark**, and **A parked head is durable and continues on any machine**.

### A parked head is durable and continues on any machine

(wink + agent, 2026-11-10, 15, and 16) A cycle's work sometimes waits off its chain, a rung's edits
set aside for an unplanned rung, or a cycle stopped for the night. Each is a head beside the
cycle's, a bushiness with a cost, worth it once the head is durable, on the remote, and continued on
this machine or another. Merged from **feat: cycle sets a rung's edits aside and takes them back**
and **Work in progress is durable and continues on any machine** (wink, 2026-11-16).

- **The set-aside** (wink + agent, 2026-11-15, from **fix: a cycle commit marks no rung current**).
  Unplanned work sets the next rung's edits aside as a jj commit with a local bookmark, and that
  cycle did it by hand: `jj restore` of the version files, `jj commit`, `jj bookmark create`, and
  `jj new` on the cycle's tip, with a `jj rebase` and a bookmark delete to take them back. The hand
  bookmark is what found the branch revset's bug, so the tool should own the steps.
  - `cycle --set-aside` saves the working copy as a commit under a local bookmark, leaves the
    version and record files out so the return cannot conflict on them, and puts `@` back on the
    cycle's tip.
  - `cycle --take-back` rebases it onto the new tip and deletes the bookmark.
  - The names follow the stage flags and are to be settled at the opening.
- **Work in progress** (wink, 2026-11-10). A cycle stopped for the night was made durable by a work
  and an agent commit titled `wip`, pushed, and removing them took two abandons and two backward
  pushes by `jj`, since `vc-x1 push` would fold the agent `@` into the last rung's agent commit. A
  scheme is wanted that makes work in progress durable, on the remote, and easy to continue on this
  machine or another, then leaves no trace in the cycle's history once the rung it belongs to is
  committed.
  - We think a separate ref, a `wip/<bookmark>` on the remote holding both `@`s, is the shape: the
    cycle's bookmark and the agent `main` never move for it, and a `continue` fetches it into `@`.
  - What the other machine's session reads is part of it: the continuation notes ride in the work
    `@` and the transcript in the agent `@`.
- **One mechanism**: name, push, fetch, take back. A parked head changes, rebased when taken back,
  so its ref is a remote bookmark, durable until deleted, not a tag, named for its cycle,
  `aside/<cycle bookmark>` or `wip/<cycle bookmark>`, and its take-back deletes it locally and on
  the remote, a push. No agent commit names a parked head until it lands through a rung.
- Once **feat: a cycle's state is recorded, and every end is durable** lands, a hand set-aside no

### feat: a cycle's state is recorded, and every end is durable

(wink + agent, 2026-11-15 and 16, from the dead-end **fix: a cycle commit marks no rung current**,
io-uring-x1's `m-13`, and zc-ring-x1's `m-14`) The cycle protocol's next form, folding the three
entries the dead-end filed, **feat: a rung's state is recorded in TODO.md**, **feat: a closing names
its shape, and its target once**, and **feat: a dead-end lands on a target or a tag**. vc-x1 infers
a cycle's commits from bookmark reachability, so a set-aside bookmark corrupted the ladder and the
commit count twice. `cycle --commit` writes the next rung `(current)`, a prediction. And a cycle
stopped early has no durable end, its agent commits' `ochid:` trailers left naming work commits no
pushed ref keeps. One cycle, its rungs below, wink's "we'll see how it goes".

- **The principle.** The repo holds what happened, and `TODO.md` holds where the cycle is going and
  which commit each finished rung is. Every stage checks that the two agree, and a disagreement
  stops it, neither side assumed right.
  - The one inference that goes is the branch revset: the cycle's commits are the change ids its
    record holds, each confirmed by the repo.
  - `zTOC.md`'s ladder is generated from the record by every cycle command, never edited by hand.
- **The record.** A fenced `toml` block follows the `###` cycle heading, and one follows each
  `#####` rung heading once the rung has started.
  - The cycle block: `bookmark`, the cycle's one bookmark, `provisional = true` while that name is
    vc-x1's placeholder, and `state`, `done` or `dead-end`, added by the closing.
  - The rung block: `state`, one of `current`, `done`, or `dead-end`, `change`, the work commit's
    full change id for `done` and `dead-end`, and `agent-at`, the agent `@`'s commit id when the
    rung started, a commit id since it changes with every snapshot.
  - `current` and `agent-at` live in the working copy alone, `--commit` replacing them, so a commit
    holds `state` and `change` only.
  - No number is stored, the ladder numbering by position.
- **The invariants**, checked by every stage before it writes:
  - Order: the opening, the `done` and `dead-end` rungs in commit order, at most one `current`, the
    rungs not started, and the closing. No rung is inserted above a done one.
  - Resolves: each `change` is one visible commit, not divergent, titled as its heading.
  - Chain: each rung's commit is the next one's parent, the last being `@-`, the tip.
  - Nothing unrecorded: `opening::@- ~ <recorded>` is empty. A hand `jj commit` in the chain is
    refused, naming the fix, and local-ladder intermediates are reported as not yet collapsed,
    `--commit` waiting for them.
  - Done is frozen (wink): a `done` or `dead-end` rung's heading and block match its own commit's,
    never deleted or changed, the prose under them editable, and vc-x1 refuses to continue until
    one changed is restored. Done rungs are not renamed, unpublished ones included.
  - Generated: `zTOC.md`'s ladder is the one the committed record or the working copy's makes, any
    other a hand edit, refused, the fix being an edit of `TODO.md`.
  - Bookmark: the cycle's bookmark is on the tip, and a move is reported.
  - Heads: vc-x1 commits on the cycle's chain alone, and `--status` reports a head forking off it.
    `--close` refuses while a work commit an agent commit names is reachable from neither the
    closing nor a pushed ref, joining it by `--close <REV,...>` or tagging it clearing that.
- **Starting a cycle.** `--open` needs nothing, and over a cycle in progress it makes nothing and
  prints the ways to end it.
  - Without `--title` the heading is the placeholder `### (untitled)`, editable until the opening
    commits, whose `--commit` refuses the placeholder. The opening's heading is then frozen and the
    closing pairs with it, the `###` heading still free to drift.
  - Without `--bookmark` the bookmark is provisional, `cycle-<ts>`, `<ts>` UTC to the second in ISO
    8601's basic form, and renamed to the title's slug when the opening commits. A name the user
    gave is never renamed.
  - `--bookmark-rename <new>` renames the cycle's bookmark on any stage, the record with it, free
    before a draft push and a push after one, its approval asked.
  - `--bookmark` on the later stages, which today names the cycle, goes, the record holding it.
- **The rung lifecycle.** A rung is any work or experiment, with the agent's help or without.
  `--rung-start` and `--rung-stop` edit `TODO.md` and `zTOC.md` in the work `@` and make no commit,
  so a rung in flight shows in the ladder.
  - `--rung-start` marks a rung `current` and records `agent-at`: the first rung not started, or
    `--title`'s, moved up to be next with its subsection. `--title X --insert` adds a heading as the
    next rung, so a ladder is built as it goes. Refused while a rung is current.
  - `--rung-stop` returns the current rung to not started, its edits left alone.
  - `--commit` commits the current rung or `--title`'s, writing `done` and `@`'s change id, and is
    refused with no rung in flight and no `--title`.
  - `--commit --dead-end` commits a rung given up, its attempt kept in history, then inserts and
    starts `revert: <rung title>`, `@` restored to the parent's tree but for the record and the
    version file, so the revert is its own reviewed commit.
  - The quick path: `--open`, `--commit --title "..."` for the opening, then for each rung
    `--rung-start --insert --title "..."`, the work, and `--commit`.
- **Scopes and pairing.** `-s u`, unpaired, joins `b`, `w`, `a`, and `p`, taken by `commit`,
  `squash`, `cycle --commit`, and `cycle --close`.
  - `u` is the work-repo of a dual workspace committed with no trailer and never covered. `p` is a
    plain repo, with no agent-repo, and stays refused on a dual workspace's sides. In a line: `p`
    says there is no agent-repo here, `u` that there is one and this commit does not involve it.
  - The scope is chosen at the commit, by what happened: `-s b` when the agent helped, `-s u` when
    it did not, and `-s w` for the N:1 case. `-s u` warns when the agent `@` differs from the
    rung's `agent-at`, a session having written during the rung.
  - The Land commits the agent `@` for the work commits with a forward `ochid:` alone, so a cycle of
    unpaired commits makes no agent commit.
  - The durability obligation starts at a paired commit: a work commit an agent commit names stays
    reachable from a pushed ref, landed, kept as a `dead-end` rung of a landed or tagged cycle, or
    tagged. An unpaired commit, or an experiment never committed, is kept or dropped freely.

  - `--close --multi-step` takes `--trapezoid [<target>]` or `--linear`, and a bare one is refused.
    `--trapezoid` takes its target from `--land <target>` when it has none, `--trapezoid A --land B`
    is refused, and `--linear` takes none. The conflicting flags are refused as they are parsed.
  - The shape is checked against the count of the recorded commits.
  - A done closing is refused while a work rung is current or not started: commit it, dead-end it,
    or delete it, a rung not started always deletable.

    restores the opening's parent tree but for the record and the version file, which still moves
    forward.

  one, and a tag is the ref for a dead-end not landed.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `--close --multi-step [--dead-end] --trapezoid\|--linear --land <target> [--push]` | the target, and its version tag | `--open` | no |
| 2 | `--close --multi-step --dead-end --tag [<name>] [--push]` | the dead-end tag | `--open --from <target>` | no |
| 3 | `--close --multi-step --dead-end --no-tag` | nothing, until a tag is pushed | `--open --from <target>` | yes |
| 4 | nothing committed | nothing needed | `--open` | no |
| 5 | outside the tool: `jj abandon`, a bookmark deleted | none | anything | cannot ask |

    `v<version>`, read by `[version]`'s `file` and `pattern`, `[land] tag = "v{version}"` setting
    the form. `--no-tag` skips it, a tag at the same commit is a no-op, one at another commit is
    refused naming both, and a workspace with no `[version]` gets none, said. A landed dead-end is
    tagged too, its version having moved forward.
  - Tags are lightweight, made by jj-lib with no git spawn, the tagged commit's title saying what it
    is.
  - The dead-end tag is named `dead-end-<ts>`, `<name>`, or `<name>-<ts>`, `<ts>` UTC to the
    millisecond in ISO 8601's basic form, `20261116T215837.123Z`, since a ref holds no `:`. A name
    taken, locally or on the remote, is refused. `--tag-dead-end <rev> [<name>]` tags a closed
    dead-end after the fact, row 3 becoming row 2.
  - A work-repo push carries the local tags `origin` lacks, listed in its plan and `--dry-run`, tags
    first, a clash stopping it. The work-repo alone is tagged, agent commits being on the agent
    `main`.

  - `--open --from <target>` follows an unlanded dead-end. It prints the dead-end's version and

  - `feat: -s u commits the work-repo unpaired`

  - Cutting the branch only at bookmarks not descending from the opening, still an inference.

content.text:
Thoughts only.

**I agree, and I'd do it before the protocol cycle.**

**What's actually work-specific:**
- **These four belong to the project, not to vc-x1.** `validate` runs the `[validate]` lists, and `build`, `run`, and `install` run the `[build]`, `[install]`, and `[profile.*]` tables. Together that's about 3,600 lines: `build_cmd.rs`, `install_cmd.rs`, `run_cmd.rs`, `command_list.rs`, and most of `validate.rs`.
  - They're language-neutral only in a weak sense: a config of shell lists with `{table.key}` placeholders. Writing that config is the project-specific part anyway, and in an xtask it's ordinary Rust instead of a small templating language.
  - The dev artifact (`vc-x1-dev` installed beside `vc-x1`) is purely vc-x1's own dogfooding. A library adopter like io-uring-x1 has nothing to install.
- **What stays in vc-x1.** The checks on vc-x1's own domain: `validate-desc`, `validate-todo`, the anchors, `validate-config`, and `validate-bot`. They check the dual-repo model and the records, not the work.
  - The `[version]` table stays too. vc-x1 reads it for the commit check, and the protocol's version tag reads it.
- **Precedent.** The version bump already moved to `cargo xtask` on the same principle: "the version is the project's".

**The set must not say `cargo xtask`.** The agent-files are carried by every adopter, so a C adopter would have `make`. They need one neutral pointer:
- A committed `[tasks]` table in `.vc-config.md` naming each command: `validate`, `validate-fast`, `install-dev`, and so on. For us those are `cargo xtask validate` and the like.
- The per-rung flow says "the project's validate, `[tasks] validate`", and the agent runs that command directly. vc-x1 doesn't run it, only documents the table in its schema.
- `custom.md` is the wrong home for this: it's local to one workspace and gitignored, and these commands belong to the project.
- **One option to weigh.** vc-x1 could keep a one-line runner, `vc-x1 task <name>`, so the agent-files can say a single command everywhere. I'd skip it, because it's the same indirection again for one fewer table lookup. If a stage ever needs to enforce "validated after the last edit", it can read `[tasks]` itself.

**What the move touches:**
- **xtask.** It gains `validate [--fast]`, `build`, `run`, and `install [--profile dev]`, at parity with today's commands, including the atomic copy-then-move install.
- **Provenance.** Today vc-x1 reads jj's `@-` and its clean or dirty state and passes them to the build through `VC_X1_BUILD_COMMIT` and `VC_X1_BUILD_STATE`. That's how the `+acd7ce44.unknown` in `-V` is made. The xtask would get it by spawning `jj`, which is the project's tool, not vc-x1's, so vc-x1's spawn register isn't involved.
- **The config.** `[validate]`, `[build]`, `[install]`, and `[profile.*]` leave the schema, and `vc-config.md` and `vc-config-model.md` regenerate. `[test] fixtures` is a question: it's vc-x1's own test plumbing and probably moves to the xtask or an environment variable.
- **The agent-files.**
  - The per-rung flow's step 4 and Dev artifact name in `versioning.md`.
  - The Long output list in `custom.md`.
  - `bash-allow.sh` already covers `cargo`.
- **The other adopters.** zc-ring-x1, iiac-perf, and io-uring-x1 each have `[validate]` lists today, so this breaks them.
  - A message to the family, plus a starter xtask shipped by the template, `../vc-x1-template`, so a Rust adopter copies it rather than writes it.
  - `vc-x1 validate` stays for one version as a refusal that names `[tasks]`, so nobody gets a silent "unknown command".

**Why before the protocol cycle:**
- The two are independent: `cycle.rs` uses none of these modules.
- The protocol cycle's docs rung rewrites the per-rung flow. Moving the tasks first means that flow names the new commands once, not twice.
- The protocol cycle runs the dev install at every rung. It's better for that loop to be on its final command from the start than to change in the middle of a long ladder.
- It's a smaller, mostly mechanical cycle, which makes a good shakedown before the big one.

**A naming wrinkle.** Once `vc-x1 validate` is freed, two different things want the name: the project's validate, and vc-x1's own record checks. Your retire-the-hyphenated-commands direction suggests folding `validate-desc`, `validate-todo`, and the rest under one command. I'd call vc-x1's `vc-x1 check`, so "validate" always means the project's. That could be this cycle or a later one.

**A rough ladder:**
1. xtask gains the tasks, at parity.
2. `[tasks]` in the config, and the agent-files and `custom.md` point at it.
3. vc-x1 drops its four commands and their config tables, leaving a refusal that names `[tasks]`.
4. The family is told, and the template gets a starter xtask.

The plain version: validate, build, run, and install are about the project's own code, so they belong in the project's `cargo xtask`. vc-x1 keeps only the checks on its repos and records. The shared agent-files point at the commands through a small `[tasks]` table in the config instead of naming `cargo xtask`, so non-Rust adopters still fit. Doing this first is cheaper, because the big protocol cycle then writes its docs and runs its dev builds against the final commands.

content.text:
Agreed. `.vc-config.md` is the repo-management config, and "how do I validate this project" isn't repo management. `custom.md` is the simplest place to start. One cost should be decided knowingly, though.

**`custom.md` is gitignored** (`.gitignore:2`).
- A fresh clone, or this project on another machine, starts with no task commands. The agent there wouldn't know to run `cargo xtask validate` until someone writes them into its `custom.md` again.
- That's acceptable today, since we work from one clone on one machine. The Long output list already lives in `custom.md` under the same limit.
- The xtask itself is committed, so the knowledge isn't lost. Only the pointer to it is local. `cargo xtask --help` lists the tasks on any clone, so the agent-files could say "the project's tasks, named in `custom.md`, else `cargo xtask --help`".

**How it fits the agent-files:**
- The per-rung flow says "the project's validate, named in `custom.md > Tasks`", and the same for the fast validate and the dev install. A `## Tasks` section makes the slot easy to find.
- The rule that `custom.md` overrides the agent-files already makes it the project layer, so this is no new mechanism. It does stretch the rule's current wording ("one machine's paths and permissions"), and the sentence would gain "and the project's task commands".
- The acquaint could check that `custom.md` names the tasks, and report it if it doesn't.

**`vc-dr-apply` needs a matching change.** Today its language skeletons append a `[validate]` table to `.vc-config.md` (`scripts/vc-dr-apply.sh:333`). After the move, a skeleton would write a `## Tasks` section into the `custom.md` it already creates. For Rust, it could ship a starter xtask too.

**Later, if clones start to matter:** your `vc-config.work.md`, a committed file beside `.vc-config.md` that holds the work's side. It's a cleaner split than either one file holding both, or the task commands living only in an ignored file. I'd wait until a second clone or machine needs it. Moving the section from `custom.md` into it later is a small edit.

**The task-move cycle, revised:**
1. The xtask gains `validate [--fast]`, `build`, `run`, and `install [--profile dev]`, at parity, provenance included.
2. `custom.md` gets `## Tasks`, and the agent-files point at it.
3. vc-x1 drops its four commands and `[validate]`, `[build]`, `[install]`, and `[profile.*]`, leaving a refusal that names `custom.md > Tasks`. `vc-dr-apply`'s skeletons follow.
4. The family is told by message.

**One decision this creates.** `custom.md` is gitignored, so it isn't in any commit. That means step 2's edit isn't reviewable in a diff, and isn't recoverable from history either. How should the cycle record what `## Tasks` says?
- I'd put the section's text in the rung subsection that adds it.
- The alternative is to treat `custom.md` edits as outside the cycle.

The plain version: yes, the commands for checking and building the project aren't repo management, so they come out of `.vc-config.md`, and `custom.md` is the easiest place to start. The catch is that `custom.md` isn't committed, so a new clone won't have the commands until someone adds them. That's fine for one machine. A committed `vc-config.work.md` can come later if it's needed.

### Durable messaging between projects

(wink, 2026-11-16) The family's members message through a shared git repo, `../vc-x1-messages`, and
a repo is a poor carrier for it. A clone of vc-x1 on fwlaptop had no `custom.md`, which is
gitignored, so its session never learned the protocol and could not send. Messaging has nothing to
do with repo management either, so neither `.vc-config.md`'s `[family]` nor `custom.md` is its home.

- What the repo costs:
  - One clone on one machine: thread and line ids are minted under that clone's `owner` mutex, so a
    second clone can mint the same ones, caught only by a rejected push (its README's What is not
    here).
  - Every member needs the repo cloned at the path its config names, and the instructions to use
    it, before it can read or send.
  - A line is final only once pushed, and the commit and push are hand steps, so lines sit
    uncommitted in one working copy, `m-12` to `m-14` today.
  - Nothing new is seen without a fetch, and nothing tells the addressed member.
- What is wanted: a message, once sent, is durable and visible from every machine and every
  member's session with no per-machine setup beyond credentials. Its id is one no two senders can
  both mint, and the pending query, what is addressed to a member and not yet answered, is kept.
- Candidates, to weigh, we think:
  - Member-scoped ids in the repo, `m-<member>-<n>`, the change its README names, keeping the repo
    and dropping the mutex.
  - A hosted tracker, a family repo's GitHub issues or discussions, read and written by `gh`, the
    server allocating ids and keeping the history, at the cost of a network dependency and the
    content living on GitHub.
  - Claude Code's own messaging between sessions, which reaches live sessions on one machine and is
    not durable, so a notifier at most.
- The instructions to take part live in a committed file, so a fresh clone has them.

I filed **Durable messaging between projects** in `TODO.md`, ranked second, right after the protocol entry, though the rank is yours to move. It covers the fwlaptop failure and what the messages repo costs:
- the single-clone `owner` mutex;
- the per-machine clone at a fixed path;
- lines that wait for hand commits and pushes;
- the fetch needed to see anything new.

It also says what "durable" should mean and lists three candidates:
- member-scoped ids in the repo;
- GitHub issues or discussions through `gh`;
- Claude Code's own messaging between sessions, as a notifier at most.

**On the work config, thoughts only.** fwlaptop shows a gap in the layers rather than a problem with `custom.md` itself. Today there are two layers:
- **The agent-files:** shared by every adopter, committed.
- **`custom.md`:** one machine's layer, gitignored on purpose. The rationale says a committed one would hand every clone of a public repo one machine's sibling paths and standing permissions.

What's missing is a **project layer**: committed, specific to this project, and not part of the shared set. Our `custom.md` already holds mostly that kind of content, which is exactly why a clone breaks:
- **Project-wide:**
  - the agent-files draft adopted locally;
  - the Long output list;
  - the pointer to the messaging protocol;
  - and, with the task move, the task commands.
- **Truly one machine's:** the standing Fetch permission, and sibling paths in general.

So I'd add a third file, your `vc-config.work.md` or similar:
- **Committed,** read after the agent-files and before `custom.md`, with `custom.md` still overriding.
- **It holds** the work's tasks, the project's conventions, and how to take part in messaging, so a fresh clone has all of them.
- **`custom.md` shrinks** to what really is local: paths, permissions, the session lock.
- **`vc-dr-apply`'s language skeletons** write its tasks section, instead of appending `[validate]` to `.vc-config.md`.
- **The acquaint** reports a missing `custom.md` when `.gitignore` names one. That would have flagged the fwlaptop clone at once, instead of messaging failing silently later.

This becomes the task-move cycle's first rung, since the tasks need somewhere committed to live. That cycle would be:
1. The committed project layer, with the project content moved out of `custom.md`.
2. The xtask gains the tasks.
3. vc-x1 drops its four commands and their tables.
4. The family is told.

Messaging stays its own entry, and only its instructions move into the new file.

The plain version: there are rules shared by every project, and settings for one machine, but nowhere committed for things specific to this project. That's why the laptop clone lost the messaging setup. A committed project file would hold the build and validate commands, the project's conventions, and the messaging instructions, so every clone has them, and `custom.md` would keep only machine-specific settings.

content.content:
## Build and install

vc-x1 is not a build system. The config says what the steps are, the build and install commands
and where the binaries land, and vc-x1 runs them in order and checks their results: it builds
before it runs or installs, reports what it is about to copy, refuses only a copy that would be
wrong, and never lets one profile's install replace another's. Cargo, not vc-x1, decides what to
rebuild.

A plain Rust crate: `cargo build` and `cargo test` of one binary, `vc-x1`, named by the
manifest's `[package].name`, which never changes. A build is chosen by a named profile, a
`[profile.<name>]` table in `.vc-config.md`, and `--profile NAME` on `build`, `run`, and `install`
picks one, else `[build] default-profile`, else `release`. The `[build] commands` list is one
build for every profile, a plain `cargo build --profile {profile.cargo} --locked` leaving its
binary in `target/`, off the PATH, so nothing a cycle builds replaces the `vc-x1` on the PATH until
the cycle lands. It is `--locked`, so every profile compiles the same dependencies, the ones
`Cargo.lock` commits. This workspace defines two profiles:

- Dev: `vc-x1 build --profile dev` runs `cargo build --profile dev --locked`, leaving the rung's
  debug binary at `target/debug/vc-x1`. After a validation it reuses the test build, so it costs
  under a second, and `vc-x1 run --profile dev` runs it first, so what runs is always the current
  code.
- Release: `vc-x1 build`, the default profile, runs `cargo build --profile release --locked`,
  leaving the release build at `target/release/vc-x1`, its `-V` naming the commit it was built
  from ([build](#build)).
- Install: at a cycle's Land, `vc-x1 install` runs the release build, which cargo skips when
  nothing changed, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin`, the `[install] dir`, after reporting what
  it is copying ([install](#install)).
- Install --profile dev: mid-cycle, `vc-x1 install --profile dev` runs the dev build, then copies
  it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1-dev`, the profile's `suffix` appended, beside the landed
  `vc-x1`, so the cycle's code can be tried from any directory
  ([install --profile](#install---profile)). Any other profile, a soak's release candidate among
  them, installs the same way under its own suffix.

Where each build leaves its binary is the config's to say, each profile's `bin`: vc-x1 never
works it out from cargo or the package's name.

The commands in the order a cycle uses them, a rung's loop first and Land after:

| Command | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| `vc-x1 validate` | fmt, clippy, every test | every rung, before review |
| `vc-x1 validate --fast` | the unit tests only | while iterating |
| `vc-x1 build --profile dev` | the dev build, into `target/debug` | to build without running |
| `vc-x1 run --profile dev` | `build --profile dev`, then runs it | trying the change |
| `vc-x1 install --profile dev` | `build --profile dev`, then copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` as `vc-x1-dev` | trying the change elsewhere |
| `vc-x1 build` | the release, the default profile, into `target/release` | at Land, or to try the release profile |
| `vc-x1 run` | `build`, then runs it | the smoke check before install |
| `vc-x1 install` | `build`, then reports it and copies it into `~/.cargo/bin` | at Land |

`validate` checks the source and makes no build of any profile. `run` and `install`, whatever the
profile, build first, as `cargo run` does, and cargo rebuilds only what changed, so the binary
`run` smoke-tests is the one `install` copies.

- `target/debug/vc-x1 -V` names the exact rung, since the version-of-record carries the cycle's
  suffix (`0.85.6-1`), and the binary banners the name it was invoked as (`argv[0]`), so a copy
  or a symlink self-reports truthfully.
- Before 2026-10-20 a cycle renamed the package to `vc-x1-dev` instead, guarded by `build.rs`
  (the single-name convention, 0.78.3, design record in `notes/chores/chores-16.md`). The rename
  and the guard are gone: a build script cannot see an install's root, and building off the PATH
  makes the rename unnecessary.

The first install, and any install when the `vc-x1` on the PATH is too old to have `install`, is
made from the source: `cargo run --locked -- install` builds the dev binary and has it build the
release and install it, report and all.

vc-x1 links jj-lib and refuses to run when the installed `jj`'s version disagrees with it
(override per invocation with `--allow-jj-mismatch`, and see `vc-x1 version`).

content.text:
Thoughts only. For a human developer, these commands would live in the project's own docs, and the agent should read the same place. An agent-only copy of "how to build and test" will drift away from the human one.

**The conventions:**
- **README.md**: what the project is, and how to install and use it. A small project also puts "Building" there.
- **CONTRIBUTING.md**: the contributor's workflow, meaning how to build, test, lint, and check before submitting. Validate, the fast validate, and the dev install are exactly that.
- **INSTALL.md**: the GNU convention for installing from source, for end users. It matters less for a `cargo install` crate.
- **The task runner itself**, our `cargo xtask` (or `make`, or `just`), is the executable truth. `cargo xtask --help` lists what exists, and the docs say which task to run when.
- **Elsewhere, AGENTS.md** is the convention for "README for agents", with setup, build, and test commands. Ours can't hold them, though, because our `AGENTS.md` is the shared set every adopter carries.

**What vc-x1 already has:** README's `## Build and install` (`README.md:75`) is that human home today. Its table lists the commands in the order a cycle uses them: validate, `--fast`, `build`/`run`/`install` with `--profile dev`, and the release at Land. After the move, the same table would list `cargo xtask ...`. That section is contributor workflow sitting inside a 2,984-line user manual, so the conventional split would be:
- **CONTRIBUTING.md `## Tasks`**: a table with columns for the task's name, its command, when to run it, and whether its output is long. That last column takes over `custom.md`'s Long output list.
- **README.md** keeps installing and using vc-x1, and links to CONTRIBUTING.md for development.

**How the shared set finds it:**
- The agent-files use task names, not commands. For example, the per-rung flow runs "the project's `validate` task" or "its `install-dev` task".
- The set names one place: "`CONTRIBUTING.md > ## Tasks`", maybe "else `README.md > ## Tasks`" for a project with no CONTRIBUTING.md. That's a fixed heading the anchor check can verify.
- `vc-dr-apply`'s language skeleton writes a CONTRIBUTING.md stub with the Rust tasks, only when the project has none, instead of appending `[validate]` to `.vc-config.md`.
- The acquaint can report a project whose Tasks table is missing a task the set uses.

**This changes the "project layer" idea.** It may not need a new file at all:
- **The tasks** go to CONTRIBUTING.md, which is committed, for humans, and read by the agent.
- **Messaging** gets its own solution, under the Todo just filed.

### A parked head is durable and continues on any machine

(wink + agent, 2026-11-10, 15, and 16) A cycle's work sometimes waits off its chain, a rung's edits
set aside for an unplanned rung, or a cycle stopped for the night. Each is a head beside the
cycle's, a bushiness with a cost, worth it once the head is durable, on the remote, and continued on
this machine or another. Merged from **feat: cycle sets a rung's edits aside and takes them back**
and **Work in progress is durable and continues on any machine** (wink, 2026-11-16).

- **The set-aside** (wink + agent, 2026-11-15, from **fix: a cycle commit marks no rung current**).
  Unplanned work sets the next rung's edits aside as a jj commit with a local bookmark, and that
  cycle did it by hand: `jj restore` of the version files, `jj commit`, `jj bookmark create`, and
  `jj new` on the cycle's tip, with a `jj rebase` and a bookmark delete to take them back. The hand
  bookmark is what found the branch revset's bug, so the tool should own the steps.
  - `cycle --set-aside` saves the working copy as a commit under a local bookmark, leaves the
    version and record files out so the return cannot conflict on them, and puts `@` back on the
    cycle's tip.
  - `cycle --take-back` rebases it onto the new tip and deletes the bookmark.
  - The names follow the stage flags and are to be settled at the opening.
- **Work in progress** (wink, 2026-11-10). A cycle stopped for the night was made durable by a work
  and an agent commit titled `wip`, pushed, and removing them took two abandons and two backward
  pushes by `jj`, since `vc-x1 push` would fold the agent `@` into the last rung's agent commit. A
  scheme is wanted that makes work in progress durable, on the remote, and easy to continue on this
  machine or another, then leaves no trace in the cycle's history once the rung it belongs to is
  committed.
  - We think a separate ref, a `wip/<bookmark>` on the remote holding both `@`s, is the shape: the
    cycle's bookmark and the agent `main` never move for it, and a `continue` fetches it into `@`.
  - What the other machine's session reads is part of it: the continuation notes ride in the work
    `@` and the transcript in the agent `@`.
- **One mechanism**: name, push, fetch, take back. A parked head changes, rebased when taken back,
  so its ref is a remote bookmark, durable until deleted, not a tag, named for its cycle,
  `aside/<cycle bookmark>` or `wip/<cycle bookmark>`, and its take-back deletes it locally and on
  the remote, a push. No agent commit names a parked head until it lands through a rung.
- Once **feat: a cycle's state is recorded, and every end is durable** lands, a hand set-aside no
  longer cuts the cycle's branch, and its `--status` reports a parked head as parked, not forked.

### feat: a cycle takes an added bookmark

(wink + agent, 2026-11-16, from **feat: a cycle's state is recorded, and every end is durable**)
`--bookmark <new>` would add a bookmark beside the cycle's own, which `--bookmark-rename` renames.
Left out of that cycle: each added bookmark invites a head off the cycle's chain, a head an agent
commit names must be made durable, and the record's change ids already address every rung. When a
need appears, it settles whether an added bookmark stays where it is made or advances, whether a
draft push carries it, and whether the Land deletes it.

A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance.
